title: Emergency Jet Fuel Import Helps Avert Shortage at Kenya's Major Airports
desc: Kenya brought in emergency jet fuel to prevent shortages at JKIA and Moi Airport as rising demand put supplies under pressure.
content:
Kenya brought in an emergency shipment of jet fuel to prevent a potential shortage at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport and Moi International Airport as rising demand placed supplies under pressure.

The country received 30,000 tonnes of Jet A-1 fuel on August 20 outside the government's usual supply arrangement, according to a fresh report on the matter.

The emergency cargo was brought in after concerns emerged that available supplies might not meet demand during August.

Demand for jet fuel had increased sharply at Kenya's two major airports, particularly at JKIA, where increased international aviation activity contributed to higher fuel consumption.

The additional shipment was intended to bridge the anticipated supply gap and ensure airlines could continue operating without major disruption.

For travellers, a jet fuel shortage could have resulted in delayed or disrupted flights. Airlines depend on reliable fuel supplies to maintain schedules, while disruptions can affect passengers, tourism, cargo and business travel.

The situation also highlights the pressure that rising aviation activity can place on Kenya's fuel supply system.

According to the report, the emergency shipment was sourced outside the normal Government-to-Government fuel supply framework after logistical challenges made it difficult to bring forward a scheduled cargo.

The next shipment under the regular arrangement was expected in early September, leaving Kenya exposed to a possible supply gap had the emergency cargo not been secured.

The special import came at a higher cost than the normal supply arrangement, underlining the financial impact of responding to an unexpected demand increase.

For Kenya's aviation sector, maintaining reliable fuel supplies is essential because JKIA serves as the country's main international gateway, while Moi International Airport plays an important role in connecting the Coast to domestic and international markets.

The emergency shipment helped prevent an immediate shortage, but the development raises broader questions about how Kenya plans for sudden increases in aviation fuel demand.

As air travel and regional aviation activity continue to change, maintaining sufficient reserves will remain important for protecting flight operations and avoiding costly disruptions.
